questions.problem:
Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+4\lambda y=0,\,y(0)={y}^{′}(1)=0,\,0\le x\le 1,\,\lambda \ge 0.
$$

Find the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues and the associated eigenfunctions of this problem.

$\,$ The eigenvalues correspond to the parameter values ${\lambda }_{n}=$  {{field-1}}, where $n\in {N}_{0}.$

$\,$ The eigenfunctions are ${y}_{n}(x)=$ {{field-2}}, where ${B}_{n}\in R.$
questions.worked_solution:
We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda >0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. 

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ 

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions $y(0)={y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ is not a parameter of the eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda >0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}+4\lambda  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $m=\pm 2\text{i}\sqrt{\lambda }.$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x\sqrt{\lambda }),\,{y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x\sqrt{\lambda })
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x\sqrt{\lambda })+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x\sqrt{\lambda }).
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(0)=0$ yields

$$
A\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)=0
$$

which gives $A=0.$ So, we have

$$
y=B\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x\sqrt{\lambda }).
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
{y}^{′}=2B\sqrt{\lambda }\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x\sqrt{\lambda }).
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields

$$
2B\sqrt{\lambda }\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\sqrt{\lambda })=0.
$$

For nontrivial solutions, we require 

$$
2\sqrt{\lambda }=\frac{\pi }{2}+n\pi =\frac{(1+2n)\pi }{2}
$$

for $n\in {N}_{0}.$ This gives the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues:

$$
{\lambda }_{n}=\frac{(1+2n)^{2}{\pi }^{2}}{16}.
$$

The corresponding eigenfunctions are 

$$
{y}_{n}(x)={B}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x\sqrt{{\lambda }_{n}}),\,{B}_{n}\in R.
$$

1.Trigonometric Eigenfunctions?

Consider the boundary value problem y″+4λy=0,y(0)=y′(1)=0,0≤x≤1,λ≥0. Find the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues and the associated eigenfunctions of this problem.

The eigenvalues correspond to the parameter values λn=
(1+2n)2π216
(1+2n)2π216
(1+4n)2π24

questions.problem:
Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}-12\lambda {y}^{′}+36{\lambda }^{2}y=0,\,{y}^{′}(1)=0,\,y(2)+6{y}^{′}(2)=0,\,1\le x\le 2,\,\lambda \in R.
$$

Find the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of this problem. Assume that $B$ and $C$ are constants.

$\,$ The eigenvalues are $\lambda =$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The eigenfunctions are $y=$ {{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda \ne 0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions.

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ and $y(2)+6{y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ is not an eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda \ne 0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-12\lambda m+36{\lambda }^{2} & =0 \\ (m-6\lambda )(m-6\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the double root $m=6\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{6\lambda x},\,{y}_{2}(x)=x{e}^{6\lambda x}
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A{e}^{6\lambda x}+Bx{e}^{6\lambda x}.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =6A\lambda {e}^{6\lambda x}+B{e}^{6\lambda x}+6B\lambda x{e}^{6\lambda x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}6A\lambda {e}^{6\lambda }+B{e}^{6\lambda }+6B\lambda {e}^{6\lambda } & =0 \\ 6A\lambda +B+6B\lambda  & =0 \\ (6\lambda )A+(1+6\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(2)+6{y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}A{e}^{12\lambda }+2B{e}^{12\lambda }+6(6A\lambda {e}^{12\lambda }+B{e}^{12\lambda }+12B\lambda {e}^{12\lambda }) & =0 \\ A+2B+6(6A\lambda +B+12B\lambda ) & =0 \\ A+2B+36A\lambda +6B+72B\lambda  & =0 \\ (1+36\lambda )A+(8+72\lambda )B & =0 \\ (1+36\lambda )A+8(1+9\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following systems of equations for $A$ and $B:$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}(6\lambda )A+(1+6\lambda )B=0 \\ (1+36\lambda )A+(8+72\lambda )B=0\end{aligned}
$$

This homogeneous linear system has a nontrivial solution if and only if the determinant is zero. This gives

$$
|\begin{aligned}6\lambda  & 1+6\lambda  \\ 1+36\lambda  & 8+72\lambda \end{aligned}|=0.
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}6\lambda (8+72\lambda )-(1+6\lambda )(1+36\lambda ) & =0 \\ 48\lambda +432{\lambda }^{2}-(1+42\lambda +216{\lambda }^{2}) & =0 \\ 216{\lambda }^{2}+6\lambda -1 & =0 \\ (12\lambda +1)(18\lambda -1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{12}\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{18}.$

Finally, we find the eigenfunction corresponding to each eigenvalue:

- Consider ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{12}.$ Then, we have the solution

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(x) & =A{e}^{6{\lambda }_{1}x}+Bx{e}^{6{\lambda }_{1}x} \\  & =A{e}^{-x/2}+Bx{e}^{-x/2}\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting ${\lambda }_{1}$ into

$$
(6\lambda )A+(1+6\lambda )B=0
$$

we get

$$
-\frac{1}{2}A+\frac{1}{2}B=0
$$

which gives $A=B,$ where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(x) & =B{e}^{-x/2}+Bx{e}^{-x/2} \\  & =B{e}^{-x/2}(x+1).\end{aligned}
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{18},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =A{e}^{6{\lambda }_{2}x}+Bx{e}^{6{\lambda }_{2}x} \\  & =A{e}^{x/3}+Bx{e}^{x/3}\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting ${\lambda }_{2}$ into

$$
(6\lambda )A+(1+6\lambda )B=0
$$

we get

$$
\frac{1}{3}A+\frac{4}{3}B=0\,⇒\,A=-4B
$$

where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =-4B{e}^{x/3}+Bx{e}^{x/3} \\  & =B{e}^{x/3}(x-4) \\  & =C{e}^{x/3}(x-4)\end{aligned}
$$

where we have set $C=B.$

So, the eigenfunctions corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively, are $B{e}^{-x/2}(x+1)\text{ and }C{e}^{x/3}(x-4).$

questions.problem:
Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}-16\lambda {y}^{′}+64{\lambda }^{2}y=0,\,{y}^{′}(0)=0,\,y(1)+2{y}^{′}(1)=0,\,0\le x\le 1,\,\lambda \in R.
$$

Find the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of this problem. Assume that $B$ and $C$ are constants.

$\,$ The eigenvalues are $\lambda =$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The eigenfunctions are $y=$ {{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda \ne 0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. 

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ 

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions ${y}^{′}(0)=0$ and $y(1)+2{y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ is not an eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda \ne 0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-16\lambda m+64{\lambda }^{2} & =0 \\ (m-8\lambda )(m-8\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the double root $m=8\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{8\lambda x},\,{y}_{2}(x)=x{e}^{8\lambda x}
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A{e}^{8\lambda x}+Bx{e}^{8\lambda x}.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =8A\lambda {e}^{8\lambda x}+B{e}^{8\lambda x}+8B\lambda x{e}^{8\lambda x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(0)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}8A\lambda +B & =0 \\ (8\lambda )A+B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(1)+2{y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}A{e}^{8\lambda }+B{e}^{8\lambda }+2(8A\lambda {e}^{8\lambda }+B{e}^{8\lambda }+8B\lambda {e}^{8\lambda }) & =0 \\ A+B+2(8A\lambda +B+8B\lambda ) & =0 \\ A+B+16A\lambda +2B+16B\lambda  & =0 \\ (1+16\lambda )A+(3+16\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following systems of equations for $A$ and $B:$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}(8\lambda )A+B=0 \\ (1+16\lambda )A+(3+16\lambda )B=0\end{aligned}
$$

This homogeneous linear system has a nontrivial solution if and only if the determinant is zero. This gives

$$
|\begin{aligned}8\lambda  & 1 \\ 1+16\lambda  & 3+16\lambda \end{aligned}|=0.
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}8\lambda (3+16\lambda )-(1)(1+16\lambda ) & =0 \\ 24\lambda +128{\lambda }^{2}-1-16\lambda  & =0 \\ 128{\lambda }^{2}+8\lambda -1 & =0 \\ (16\lambda -1)(8\lambda +1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{8}\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{16}.$

Finally, we find the eigenfunction corresponding to each eigenvalue:

- Consider ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{8}.$ Then, we have the solution

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(x) & =A{e}^{8{\lambda }_{1}x}+Bx{e}^{8{\lambda }_{1}x} \\  & =A{e}^{-x}+Bx{e}^{-x}\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting ${\lambda }_{1}$ into

$$
(8\lambda )A+B=0
$$

 
we get 

$$
-A+B=0\,⇒\,A=B
$$

where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=B{e}^{-x}(x+1).
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{16},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =A{e}^{8{\lambda }_{2}x}+Bx{e}^{8{\lambda }_{2}x} \\  & =A{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2}\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting ${\lambda }_{2}$ into

$$
(8\lambda )A+B=0
$$

 
we get 

$$
\frac{1}{2}A+B=0\,⇒\,A=-2B
$$

where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =-2B{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2} \\  & =B{e}^{x/2}(x-2) \\  & =C{e}^{x/2}(x-2)\end{aligned}
$$

where we have set $C=B.$

So, the eigenfunctions corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively, are $B{e}^{-x}(x+1)\text{ and }C{e}^{x/2}(x-2).$

questions.problem:
Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+25{\lambda }^{2}y=0,\,y(0)=0,\,{y}^{′}(2)=0,\,0\le x\le 2,\,\lambda \ge 0.
$$

Find the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues and the associated eigenfunctions of this problem.

$\,$ The eigenvalues correspond to the parameter values ${\lambda }_{n}=$ {{field-1}}, where $n\in N.$

$\,$ The eigenfunctions are ${y}_{n}(x)=$ {{field-2}}, where ${B}_{n}\in R.$
questions.worked_solution:
We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda \ne 0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. 

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ 

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions $y(0)=0$ and ${y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ does not correspond to an eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda >0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}+25{\lambda }^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $m=\pm 5\text{i}\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\lambda x),\,{y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\lambda x)
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\lambda x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\lambda x).
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(0)=0$ yields

$$
A\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)=0
$$

which gives $A=0.$ So, we have

$$
y=B\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\lambda x).
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
{y}^{′}=5B\lambda \operatorname{cos}⁡(5\lambda x).
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields

$$
5B\lambda \operatorname{cos}⁡(10\lambda )=0.
$$

For nontrivial solutions, we require 

$$
10\lambda =\frac{\pi }{2}+n\pi =\frac{(2n+1)\pi }{2}
$$

for $n\in N.$ This gives the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues:

$$
{\lambda }_{n}=\frac{(2n+1)\pi }{20}.
$$

The corresponding eigenfunctions are 

$$
{y}_{n}(x)={B}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5{\lambda }_{n}x),\,{B}_{n}\in R.
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+25\lambda y=0,\,{y}^{′}(0)={y}^{′}(\pi )=0,\,0\le x\le \pi ,\,\lambda \ge 0.
$$

Find the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues and the associated eigenfunctions of this problem.

$\,$ The eigenvalues correspond to the parameter values ${\lambda }_{n}=$ {{field-1}}, where $n\in N.$

$\,$ The eigenfunctions are ${y}_{n}(x)=$ {{field-2}}, where ${B}_{n}\in R.$
questions.worked_solution:
We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda >0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. 

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ 

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions ${y}^{′}(0)={y}^{′}(\pi )=0$ yields $A=0.$ Thus, we have a nontrivial solution, so $\lambda =0$ is a parameter corresponding to the eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda >0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}+25\lambda  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $m=\pm 5\text{i}\sqrt{\lambda }.$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x\sqrt{\lambda }),\,{y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x\sqrt{\lambda })
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x\sqrt{\lambda })+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x\sqrt{\lambda }).
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
{y}^{′}=-5A\sqrt{\lambda }\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x\sqrt{\lambda })+5B\sqrt{\lambda }\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x\sqrt{\lambda }).
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(0)=0$ yields

$$
-5A\sqrt{\lambda }\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+5B\sqrt{\lambda }\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)=0
$$

which gives $B=0.$ So, we have

$$
y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x\sqrt{\lambda }).
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(\pi )=0$ yields

$$
-5A\sqrt{\lambda }\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\pi \sqrt{\lambda })=0.
$$

For nontrivial solutions, we require 

$$
5\pi \sqrt{\lambda }=n\pi 
$$

for $n\in N.$ This gives the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues:

$$
{\lambda }_{n}=\frac{{n}^{2}}{25}.
$$

The corresponding eigenfunctions are 

$$
{y}_{n}(x)={B}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x\sqrt{{\lambda }_{n}}),\,{B}_{n}\in R.
$$

Consider the boundary value problem y″+25λy=0,y′(0)=y′(π)=0,0≤x≤π,λ≥0. Find the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues and the associated eigenfunctions of this problem.

The eigenvalues correspond to the parameter values λn=
n225
n225
n25
n250
n210
, where n∈N.

The eigenfunctions are yn(x)=
Bncos⁡(5xλn)
Bncos⁡(5xλn)
Bnsin⁡(5xλn)
Bncos⁡(xλn)
Bnsin⁡(xλn)
, where Bn∈R.
